episodes.title: Why Your Game Screen Splits in Two
episodes.thesis: Screen tearing appears when one display refresh contains portions of different rendered frames.
frames: That horizontal split is not your GPU failing. It is two finished frames sharing one display refresh.
A fixed-refresh screen scans a new image on its own clock, line by line from top to bottom.
The GPU finishes frames on a different schedule, and scene complexity changes that delivery time from moment to moment.
If the displayed buffer changes mid-scan, the upper lines can show one frame while lower lines show the next.
V-Sync waits for a refresh boundary, while variable refresh rate changes the display timing to meet a finished frame.
So tearing is a presentation mismatch, not a broken texture or low resolution. Two clocks simply crossed mid-picture.

episodes.title: Why V-Sync Can Make Controls Feel Slower
episodes.thesis: V-Sync can add waiting because a completed frame must meet a display refresh boundary.
frames: V-Sync can remove the visible tear, yet the same setting may make a fast game feel slightly less immediate.
With synchronisation enabled, a completed frame is presented on the display's refresh boundary instead of arriving whenever it finishes.
Miss that boundary by a fraction and the previous image may remain visible until another refresh opportunity arrives.
At sixty hertz one refresh lasts about sixteen point seven milliseconds. At one hundred and twenty, it is roughly eight point three.
A deep frame queue can add more waiting because fresh input sits behind work the CPU prepared earlier.
V-Sync is therefore a trade-off, not a fixed lag number: tear-free presentation in exchange for timing that needs careful pacing.

episodes.title: How VRR Makes a Monitor Wait for the GPU
episodes.thesis: Variable refresh rate lets a compatible display follow GPU frame delivery inside a supported timing window.
frames: Variable refresh rate does not make the GPU faster. It changes when a compatible monitor begins its next refresh.
A fixed display keeps ticking at one rate, even while game frames finish early, late or somewhere between.
With VRR, the monitor can refresh when the next frame is ready, reducing repeated frames, stutter and tearing inside its range.
That range has limits. A display might vary between sixty-four and one hundred and twenty hertz, not from zero to infinity.
Fall below the lower bound and frames may be repeated. Exceed the top and familiar fixed-refresh constraints return.
VRR is therefore timing flexibility, not free performance. The GPU, display, connection and presentation path must all support it.

episodes.title: Why HDR Games Still Need Tone Mapping
episodes.thesis: Tone mapping adapts a game's wide luminance range to the real brightness limits of the attached display.
frames: An HDR game can calculate brighter highlights and deeper contrast than one real screen can reproduce at the same time.
The renderer knows the scene's light values, while the display reports minimum, maximum and full-frame brightness limits.
Tone mapping bends that wide range into the output range, deciding how highlights, mid-tones and dark detail share the available brightness.
Simply clipping everything above the panel limit would turn bright clouds, sparks or reflections into flat white patches.
Different displays have different capabilities, so the same scene may need a different curve to preserve its intended balance.
HDR is not just more brightness. Tone mapping is the controlled compromise that decides which light survives on this screen.

episodes.title: How Anti-Aliasing Removes Stair-Step Edges
episodes.thesis: Anti-aliasing estimates partial coverage or combines image evidence so diagonal geometry does not collapse into hard pixel steps.
frames: A perfectly straight diagonal can look like a staircase in a game because the screen still draws a square pixel grid.
Without anti-aliasing, each edge pixel becomes fully covered or fully empty, creating a hard sequence of visible steps.
MSAA checks several sub-pixel coverage positions, letting an edge pixel represent a blend instead of a binary answer.
FXAA searches the finished image for jagged patterns and smooths them quickly, though fine detail can become softer.
Temporal methods borrow evidence from earlier frames, improving stability but risking ghosting when history no longer matches motion.
So anti-aliasing is not one filter. Every method trades cleaner edges against cost, softness or artefacts across time.

episodes.title: Why Motion Blur Can Make 30 FPS Look Smoother
episodes.thesis: Motion blur spreads a moving object across its path, softening visible jumps without creating new simulation updates.
frames: Motion blur cannot create extra frames, yet it can make the movement between existing frames feel less harsh.
A real camera gathers light while its shutter is open, so a fast object leaves a streak across that exposure.
Games often estimate the same path with per-pixel velocity, then sample and blend colour along the direction of travel.
That spread hides some of the step between two positions, which can make thirty frames per second look more continuous.
It does not update controls sooner, repair a stutter or perfectly handle every reflection, shadow and crossing object.
Motion blur is therefore visual glue, not more performance. It can soften the gap, while the game still updates at the same rate.

episodes.title: How Frame Generation Creates In-Between Frames
episodes.thesis: Frame generation synthesises intermediate images between rendered frames without adding new game simulation or input samples.
frames: Frame generation can make motion look much smoother, but the new image between two frames was not fully rendered by the game.
The system examines consecutive frames plus motion evidence such as optical flow, motion vectors, depth and camera data.
It predicts where visible pixels belong between those moments, then synthesises an intermediate image for the display.
The displayed frame rate rises, while game simulation and input sampling still follow the underlying rendered frames.
Interpolation also needs careful pacing and can distort rapid motion, scene changes or interface elements when its evidence is weak.
Frame generation is best understood as visual interpolation: smoother presentation built on top of a healthy base frame rate.
